fallback.text: A butterfly starts as a tiny egg.

ladder: Let’s think about the very beginning.
Which one is the smallest of all?
The caterpillar has to come out of something.
It comes out of a tiny egg on a leaf.
A tiny egg comes first. Tap "A tiny egg".

presentation.prompt: A butterfly starts very small. What comes first of all?

fallback.text: We plant leafy plants for caterpillars and flowers for butterflies.

presentation.speaker: Chatty the Parrot
presentation.text: So we need leafy plants too, for the caterpillars to munch, and flowers for the butterflies to drink from. In go the seeds, and out comes the water.

fallback.text: The butterfly garden is planted again.

presentation.text: The butterfly garden is planted again, with rows of flowers and leafy green plants.

fallback.text: You planted the whole garden!

presentation.text: You planted the whole garden! Now we wait and watch.

fallback.text: There is a door with no handle behind the last bookshelf.

presentation.speaker: Keeper Quill
presentation.text: Behind the last bookshelf there is a door with no handle, no keyhole, and no hinges you can see. I have never opened it. Perhaps you can.

fallback.text: The note points to a pattern in the carved stars above the door.

ladder: Good reading! Let’s look at the note again.
The note says the door is "not pulled", so it is not about handles or keys.
It says the door "listens for" something.
Read the last three words: "the stars above it".
The note points to a pattern in the carved stars. Choose that one.

options.label: A pattern in the carved stars above the door
A key hidden somewhere in the library
A magic word to shout at the door

presentation.prompt: A folded note is tucked into the frame. It reads: "The door has no handle, for it is not pulled. It listens for the pattern of the stars above it." What does the note tell us to look for?

fallback.text: The diary page came first, then the map, then the note.

ladder: Nice work. Think about the story these clues tell.
Something has to be built before anyone can write directions to it.
The diary page is about building the door, so it came first.
Then someone marked the shelf on a map.
Diary page, then map, then the note about the stars.

items.label: A map of the library, marked "the last shelf"
The folded note about the stars
A diary page: "Today we built a door"

presentation.prompt: Three clues were left behind, each dated. Put them in the order they were written.

fallback.text: 5 stars and 4 stars make 9 carved stars.

ladder: You can do this. There are two rows to add.
Hold the 5 from the top row in your head.
Count on 4 more: 6, 7, 8, 9.
5 and 4 make nine.
There are 9 carved stars. Type 9 to keep going.

presentation.prompt: Above the door there are 5 carved stars in the top row and 4 in the bottom row. How many carved stars are there altogether?

fallback.text: You have gathered all three clues.

presentation.speaker: Keeper Quill
presentation.text: Nine stars, three clues, and a door that listens. You have found more in one afternoon than I have in years.

fallback.text: The three clues are pinned on the library wall.

presentation.text: The three clues are pinned side by side on the library wall, under the nine carved stars.

fallback.text: You gathered every clue!

presentation.text: You gathered every clue! Now you know what the door is waiting for: a pattern.

fallback.text: The carvings go star, moon, star, moon, star, and then one worn smooth.

presentation.speaker: Keeper Quill
presentation.text: Look closely at the carvings. They are not all stars. Star, moon, star, moon, star, and then one carving worn too smooth to read.

fallback.text: The pattern takes turns, so the worn carving is a moon.

ladder: You are close. Say the carvings out loud in order.
Star, moon, star, moon, star.
Two shapes keep taking turns.
Every star is followed by a moon.
The worn carving is a moon. Choose the moon.

presentation.prompt: Star, moon, star, moon, star. Which carving must the worn one be?

fallback.text: Short silver, then medium iron, then long brass.

ladder: Careful measuring wins here.
Hold the rods side by side in your mind.
Which rod would disappear into the deepest slot?
The silver rod is shortest and the brass rod is longest.
Short silver, then medium iron, then long brass.

presentation.prompt: Three slots open in the door, each a different depth. Put the rods in order from shortest to longest.

fallback.text: "Ajar" means open a little way.

ladder: New word! Let’s work it out from the sentence.
The door swings, so something is moving.
A locked door cannot swing at all.
It is open, but only a little way.
"Ajar" means open a little way. Choose that one.

presentation.prompt: The door swings ajar. What does "ajar" mean?

fallback.text: The door swings ajar and warm light spills out.

presentation.speaker: Keeper Quill
presentation.text: The rods slide home, the moon carving glows for a moment, and the door swings ajar. Warm light spills out across the library floor.

fallback.text: The secret door stands open.

presentation.text: The secret door stands open, and the passage behind it is lit again.

fallback.text: You opened the secret door!

presentation.text: You solved the pattern lock and opened the door! Time to see what is inside.

fallback.text: Nella needs help feeding the creatures at the cove.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: Good morning! Everyone here is hungry, and I only have two hands. Will you help me feed them?

fallback.text: The turtle eats the green weed.

ladder: Look at the buckets. One of them is green.
The turtle eats green weed, so we want the green one.
The bucket of green weed is the one. Tap it to bring it over.

presentation.prompt: The little sea turtle eats green weed. Which bucket should we bring her?

fallback.text: Two crabs need 2 fish.

ladder: Count the crabs with me. One crab, two crabs.
Each crab gets one fish, so we need the same number of fish as crabs.
There are two crabs, so we need 2 fish. Tap the two fish.

presentation.prompt: Two crabs are waiting, and each crab gets one fish. How many fish do we need?

fallback.text: We leave the food and let the sleeping seal rest.

ladder: How do you feel when someone wakes you up too soon?
A sleepy seal is a growing seal. Her food can wait for her.
We leave her food and let her sleep. Tap that one.

options.label: Leave her food and let her sleep

presentation.prompt: The baby seal is fast asleep in her warm pen. What should we do?

fallback.text: Everyone at the cove has been fed.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: Everybody is fed, and nobody got the wrong breakfast. You are a good helper.

fallback.text: The creatures at the cove have been fed.

presentation.text: The care pens are full of happy noises. Every creature at the cove has had breakfast.

fallback.text: Nella needs help with the morning care round.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: Every morning I do the care round: fresh water, food, a check on each pen, and then the log book. Come and do it with me.

fallback.text: Three pens with two buckets each need 6 buckets.

ladder: Take your time. Count the pens first, then the buckets each one needs.
Three pens, and every pen wants two buckets.
Count two for the first pen, two for the second, two for the third.
That is 2 and 2 and 2 altogether.
Two, four, six. We carry 6 buckets. Choose that one.

presentation.prompt: There are three care pens, and each pen needs two buckets of fresh water. How many buckets do we carry?

fallback.text: Water first, then food, then the check, then the log book.

ladder: Think about the very first thing a thirsty creature needs.
Clean water comes before food, so nobody eats in a dirty pen.
After feeding, Nella walks past every pen to see how everyone looks.
Writing it down is always last, because you can only write what already happened.
The order is water, then food, then the check, then the log book.

items.label: Fill every pen with fresh water
Give each creature its own food
Write what happened in the log book

presentation.prompt: Put the care round in the order Nella does it.

fallback.text: The turtle needs deeper water in her pen.

ladder: Watch where she bumps. It is always the shallow end.
A turtle swims. What happens when the water is too shallow to swim in?
She keeps running out of water before she runs out of swimming.
She is asking for deeper water. Choose that answer.

options.label: She needs deeper water to swim in
Turtles bump into things for no reason

presentation.prompt: The sea turtle keeps bumping her nose on the shallow end of her pen. What is she telling us?

fallback.text: Nella writes the care round in her log book.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: Water, food, a good look at everyone, and now the log book. I am writing down what you noticed about the turtle. That is how she gets a deeper pen tomorrow.

fallback.text: The creatures at the cove have been cared for.

presentation.text: Every pen at the cove holds clean water and a fed, settled creature. The log book has today on its page.

fallback.text: Nella needs help planning the food supply at the cove.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: The supply boat only comes every few days, so I have to plan the food instead of guessing. Work the numbers through with me and we will get it right.

fallback.text: The cove uses 23 pieces of food a day.

ladder: Take your time. Two numbers are given, and you need their total.
One day of food is the turtle’s share added to the seal’s share.
Set it out as 14 + 9.
14 + 6 is 20, and there are 3 more to add.
The cove uses 23 pieces a day. Type 23 to keep going.

presentation.prompt: The log book says the sea turtle eats 14 pieces of food a day and the seal eats 9. How many pieces does the cove use in one day?

fallback.text: There are 17 pieces of food left in the crate.

ladder: Good. Now take today’s round out of what the crate held.
What is left is the gap between 40 and one day of food, so this is a subtraction.
Set it out as 40 - 23.
23 plus 7 is 30, and 10 more makes 40.
There are 17 pieces left. Type 17 to keep going.

presentation.prompt: The supply crate started this morning with 40 pieces. After today’s round, how many pieces are left?

fallback.text: 17 pieces is less than the 46 needed for two days, so the cove would run short.

ladder: Compare two numbers: what is left, and what two more days would cost.
Two days at 23 pieces each is 23 + 23.
That is 46 pieces needed, and the crate holds 17.
Is 17 bigger or smaller than 46?
17 is far smaller than 46, so the cove runs short. Choose that answer.

options.label: The cove will run short before the boat arrives
The food will last exactly until the boat arrives
There will be food left over when the boat arrives

presentation.prompt: The supply boat arrives in two more days, and each day costs 23 pieces. What should Nella expect from the 17 pieces left?

fallback.text: Two days plus a spare day is 69 pieces.

ladder: Read the rule again. It asks for two things added together.
Two days of food, and then one spare day on top.
A day is 23 pieces, so start with 23 + 23 for the two days.
That is 46, and the spare day adds one more 23.
46 + 23 is 69, so she orders 69 pieces. Choose that one.

presentation.prompt: Nella’s rule is to order enough for every day until the boat returns, plus one spare day. The boat returns in two days. How many pieces should she order?

fallback.text: Nella orders 69 pieces of food for the cove.

presentation.speaker: Nella the cove keeper
presentation.text: Sixty nine it is, and a spare day so nobody here ever waits for a boat. You planned that with numbers instead of hoping. That is the whole job.

fallback.text: The creatures at the cove have been cared for.

presentation.text: The care round is done and the order is written. Every pen at the cove is fed, and the crate will not run empty.

fallback.text: The lighthouse lamp is dark. Its machine needs crystals.

presentation.speaker: Chatty the Parrot
presentation.text: The big lamp at the top of the lighthouse has gone dark. Inside, there is a machine with empty slots. It needs its glowing crystals back!

fallback.text: Count the empty slots on the machine.

ladder: Let us count the empty slots together.
Point at each empty slot on the machine.
Count them out loud: one, two...
There is one more slot after two.
There are three slots. Tap "Three slots".

presentation.prompt: Look at the machine. How many empty slots need a crystal?

fallback.text: The lighthouse is turning again.

presentation.text: Deep under the floor something heavy begins to turn. The great lamp glows, then blazes, and a beam sweeps out across the water. Far off, a ship sounds its horn.

fallback.text: You lit the lighthouse.

presentation.text: You lit the lighthouse! The harbor gate is open now. There is a marketplace just past the docks.

fallback.text: The lighthouse machine needs nine units of power. Each crystal gives three units.

presentation.speaker: The Harbor Master
presentation.text: No ship can come in while the lighthouse is dark, so the gate stays shut. The machine inside needs nine units of power before the lamp will turn. Every crystal you slot in gives three units.

fallback.text: Nine units are needed and each crystal gives three.

ladder: One crystal gives three units. Is that enough for nine?
Try counting up in threes: three, six...
Three, six, nine. How many numbers did you say?
You counted three numbers to reach nine.
Three crystals give nine units. The answer is 3.

presentation.prompt: The lamp needs 9 units of power. Each crystal gives 3 units. How many crystals should you slot in?

fallback.text: The lighthouse is turning again.

presentation.text: Deep under the floor something heavy begins to turn. The great lamp glows, then blazes, and a beam sweeps out across the water. Far off, a ship sounds its horn.

fallback.text: The lighthouse turns again and the harbor gate is open.

presentation.text: The beam is sweeping the water again and the harbor gate has swung open. The Harbor Master says the marketplace is just past the docks, and that something odd has been happening there.

fallback.text: The lamp needs ten units. The gauge reads four. Each crystal is worth three units.

presentation.speaker: The Harbor Master
presentation.text: The lamp will not turn under ten units of power. The gauge on the machine reads four, and it has been stuck there since the trouble started. There is a crate of crystals by the stairs, and each one is worth three units.

fallback.text: Work out the gap between four units and ten units.

ladder: You are looking for the gap between what it has and what it needs.
Start at four and count up to ten.
Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. How many steps was that?
Ten take away four is what you want.
The machine still needs 6 units.

presentation.prompt: The lamp needs 10 units and the gauge already reads 4. How many more units does the machine still need?

fallback.text: Six units are needed and each crystal gives three.

ladder: One crystal gives three. Is one enough for six?
Try counting up in threes until you reach six.
Three, six. That is two steps.
Two crystals give three and three.
Two crystals cover six units. The answer is 2.

presentation.prompt: Each crystal is worth 3 units. How many crystals will cover those 6 units?

fallback.text: The lighthouse is turning again.

presentation.text: Deep under the floor something heavy begins to turn. The great lamp glows, then blazes, and a beam sweeps out across the water. Far off, a ship sounds its horn.

fallback.text: The lighthouse turns again and the harbor gate is open.

presentation.text: The beam sweeps the water again and the harbor gate swings open. The Harbor Master is already worrying about something else: one of the Great Harbor Gears has gone missing from the marketplace.

learningObjectives.title: Understanding cause and effect in nature
Careful observation of the natural world
Learning how animals live and behave
Sorting things by what they are

wonderWallQuestions.question: How does a caterpillar become a butterfly?
